final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

3. **4-week plan** — written out week by week in the report and in the subtask.

Only thing left is the phone call to book an eval, which only you can do — left as a `waiting` subtask with the number and talking points. Parent task set to `waiting` since that's the only open item.

report.markdown:
## Training Plan: Border Collie Mix (14mo rescue) — Leash Pulling + Dog Reactivity

### 1. Hire a trainer, or DIY?
**Hybrid recommendation:** DIY the leash-pulling (a mechanical skill you can teach yourself), but get a professional eval for the dog-reactivity piece specifically. Reactivity is easy to accidentally reinforce or worsen if the timing/distance work is off, and a 14-month adolescent rescue is still forming associations — worth getting one expert set of eyes on it early. Start the 4-week DIY plan below immediately either way; layer in the trainer for reactivity once booked.

### 2. Local South Bay trainer options (real prices)

| Trainer | Method | Price | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **D For Dogz** (dfordogtraining.com) — 650-538-3011 | Positive reinforcement | Not listed online, call for quote (market rate ~$150-300/session in Bay Area) | Explicitly runs leash-reactive classes; testimonials describe dogs with this exact profile (barking/lunging at other dogs on leash). Covers San Jose, Sunnyvale, Santa Clara, Mountain View, Palo Alto. **Top pick.** |
| **Bay Area Dog Training** (bayareadogtraining.com) | Obedience-focused, praise-based (not food) | $55 home evaluation; weekly ~45-min private lessons; $400/7-week group add-on | <cite index="17-2,17-3">Each Private Lesson package focuses on walking on a loose leash while also learning the obedience commands of sit, down, stand and stay, with each private lesson approximately 45 minutes, once a week.</cite> Good for the pulling piece; confirm they handle reactivity before booking. |
| **Off Leash K9 Training – San Jose** (dogtrainerssanjose.com) | E-collar/balanced | <cite index="1-1,1-2">First lesson $500 (includes e-collar, 20ft leash), then $100/session after</cite>; <cite index="1-5,1-6">an 8-lesson program for dogs with aggression or reactivity issues around other dogs, including the basic obedience package plus additional lessons around other dogs</cite> — roughly $1,200 total. Pricier, uses aversive tools — backup option only. |

**Action for you:** Call D For Dogz first (650-538-3011), mention the leash-reactivity and ask about evening/weekend slots and pricing. Bay Area Dog Training as a second quote for comparison.

### 3. Four-week DIY plan (evenings/weekends)

**Week 1 — Foundations, low distraction**
- Switch to a front-clip harness or head halter to cut pulling power immediately.
- Teach "look at me" and hand-target with high-value treats, 2x/day, 5-10 min, indoors/backyard.
- Practice loose-leash walking in a quiet driveway/street: reward every step beside you, stop the moment leash tightens ("be a tree").
- Identify your dog's reactivity threshold distance — the distance at which he notices another dog without reacting. Stay at/beyond that distance on all walks this week.

**Week 2 — Engagement + counter-conditioning**
- Continue loose-leash drills on real walk routes (15-20 min).
- At threshold distance, the instant he sees another dog (before any bark), mark and feed continuously until the dog passes — building a "other dogs = treats" association.
- Teach an emergency U-turn cue for when distance can't be controlled.
- Keep walks short; end on success rather than pushing through stress.

**Week 3 — Gradually close distance**
- Only if week 2 showed consistent calm at threshold, shrink the distance by 5-10 ft increments, rewarding calm looks.
- Add loose-leash practice in slightly busier settings (a quiet park, new block).
- If reactivity is still consistent, hold distance steady and lean on the trainer eval instead of pushing closer.

**Week 4 — Consolidate**
- Combine loose-leash + reactivity work on normal walks, rewarding calm passing at whatever distance currently works.
- Consider brief calm greetings only with known, calm dogs — skip otherwise.
- Reassess: pulling should be noticeably reduced in low-distraction settings; reactivity should show longer calm-before-bark and faster recovery. Use this to decide whether to keep going solo or shift more of the reactivity work to the trainer.

**Throughout:** stay positive-reinforcement only — never punish barking/lunging, which tends to worsen fear-based reactivity. Keep every family member using the same cues/rules for consistency.

### Next steps (yours to do)
- Call D For Dogz (650-538-3011) and/or Bay Area Dog Training to book an evaluation, mentioning evening/weekend availability only.
- Begin Week 1 steps this weekend regardless of trainer scheduling.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire trainer vs DIY
subtasks.description:
Decision: Hire a trainer for the reactivity piece, DIY the leash-pulling piece.

Reasoning: Leash pulling alone is a mechanical skill (loose-leash walking) that a consistent owner can teach solo in a few weeks with standard positive-reinforcement techniques — no need to pay for this alone. But barking/reacting at every other dog on walks is textbook leash reactivity, and getting the timing, distance thresholds, and counter-conditioning wrong can accidentally reinforce the behavior or escalate it. A 14-month adolescent rescue is also still forming its relationship with new triggers, so getting it right early matters.

Recommended path: Start the loose-leash-walking piece yourself immediately (see 4-week plan). In parallel, book one evaluation/consult with a positive-reinforcement trainer experienced in reactivity (see trainer options subtask) to get a customized desensitization protocol for the dog-reactivity specifically, then continue that piece under their guidance (private lessons, not necessarily a long expensive package). This blends DIY savings with professional guidance where the risk of doing it wrong is highest.

Phone: 650-538-3011. No price listed online — call for quote (per general market rates for private in-home behavior work in the Bay Area, expect roughly $150–$300/session).
3. Bay Area Dog Training (bayareadogtraining.com) - $55 in-home evaluation fee; private lesson package includes weekly ~45-min sessions focused on loose-leash walking + obedience; add-on group classes at $400 for a 7-week session. Uses physical praise, not food-reward based.

Recommendation: Call D For Dogz first (positive reinforcement, explicit reactive-dog experience, testimonials matching this exact profile of dog-reactive barking/lunging) and Bay Area Dog Training for a lower-cost comparison quote. Off Leash K9 is pricier and uses e-collar methods — only consider if the others don't fit.

subtasks.title: Draft week-by-week training plan (weeks 1-4)
subtasks.description:
Week-by-week plan for weeks 1-4, evenings/weekends, for a 14-month rescue border collie mix that pulls on leash and barks at other dogs.

WEEK 1 — Foundations at low distraction
- Switch to front-clip harness (e.g., Easy Walk) or head halter to reduce pulling power immediately (equipment change, not training, but makes weeks 1-4 physically manageable).
- Indoors/backyard: teach "look at me" / name-recognition and hand-target cue with high-value treats (small pieces of chicken/cheese), 5-10 min sessions, 2x/day.
- Start loose-leash walking in the driveway/quiet street: reward every step the dog stays beside you; stop moving the instant the leash goes tight ("be a tree").
- Identify the dog's reactivity threshold distance: on a walk, note the distance at which the dog first notices another dog without reacting. Stay at or beyond that distance for now — do not push closer.

WEEK 2 — Build engagement + start counter-conditioning
- Continue loose-leash drills, now on actual walk routes, short 15-20 min walks.
- Begin counter-conditioning at threshold distance: the moment the dog sees another dog (before it barks), mark and feed a treat continuously until the other dog passes ("Look at That" / Pattern Games style). Goal: dog starts associating other dogs with treats, not alarm.
- Practice "U-turn"/emergency turn cue to calmly exit situations where distance can't be controlled.
- Keep sessions short and end on a success — better to do 3 short walks than 1 long stressful one.

WEEK 3 — Decrease distance gradually
- Only if week 2 showed consistent calm behavior at threshold distance, begin decreasing distance to other dogs by small increments (5-10 ft at a time), always rewarding calm looks.
- Add loose-leash walking in slightly busier environments (quiet park, different block).
- Continue daily 2x short training sessions on hand-target/look-at-me to keep engagement sharp.
- If the dog still reacts consistently, do NOT decrease distance — hold at week 2 distance and get a trainer eval (see hire-trainer subtask).

WEEK 4 — Consolidate and generalize
- Combine loose-leash walking + reactivity work on real walks: reward calm passing of other dogs at whatever distance is currently manageable.
- Introduce brief on-leash greetings only if the dog is consistently calm at close range with calm, known dogs — otherwise skip this for now.
- Assess progress: pulling should be reduced on cue in low-distraction settings; reactivity should show longer calm-looking before any bark, and faster recovery after seeing a dog.
- Use this week's outcome to decide whether to continue DIY, or move into private trainer sessions for the reactivity piece (see hiring subtask) if progress has stalled.

General notes: keep all sessions positive-reinforcement based (treats/praise), never punish barking/lunging (this can worsen fear-based reactivity). Consistency across both walkers/family members matters — everyone should use the same cues and rules.

Mention: 14-month rescue border collie mix, pulls on leash, barks/reacts at every other dog seen on walks. Ask about evening/weekend availability since that's all you have.
